The paper presents a stochastic optimization framework for reducing turbofan noise by determining optimal acoustic liner impedance.
The stochastic optimization problem is formulated based on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) measure to determine a robust optimal impedance factor.
A parallel reduced-order modeling framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) is developed to dramatically improve the computational efficiency of the stochastic optimization solver.
The reduced stochastic optimization problem can be solved in less than 500 seconds, whereas the computation of the full-order Helmholtz solutions would be computationally forbidding.

The numerical experiments show that with 95% certainty, the acoustic noise energy can be optimally controlled within 48.66% of the noise level associated with the hard-wall condition without an acoustic liner.
The paper considers uncertainties in the acoustic wavenumber due to variability in weather conditions, and in the fan noise source amplitude due to incomplete knowledge.
The POD basis is constructed by solving the full-order Helmholtz equation for a set of parameter samples and determining the optimal POD basis that can best approximate these snapshots.
POD is the most efficient method for reduced-order modeling of the non-coercive Helmholtz equation, as it does not require computing the inf-sup constant needed by the greedy reduced basis method.

The realistic nacelle geometry used in the simulations has a fan radius of 1.2 m, an acoustic liner length of 1.08 m starting at 0.21 m from the fan plane, and a far-field boundary 5 m away from the fan noise source.
The wavenumber range considered is Λ = [5, 10], corresponding to wavelengths λ = 2π/k ∈ [0.2π, 0.4π], and the mesh resolution is chosen to have about 10 points per wavelength.

The parallel computation of the cost function involves each processor independently solving the reduced-order Helmholtz equation for its assigned random samples, and then communicating the noise energy values to sum them up.
The paper provides well-posedness and finite element error analyses of the state system and optimization problem.
The stochastic optimization problem is solved using a BFGS quasi-Newton method with a line search based on cubic interpolation and the Armijo condition.
The reduced-order modeling approach dramatically reduces the computational cost of the stochastic optimization solver, enabling it to be solved within 500 seconds.
The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the stochastic optimization framework and the parallel reduced-order modeling approach for turbofan noise reduction.
